**René François Ghislain Magritte** (French: [[ʁəne fʁɑ̃swa ɡilɛ̃ maɡʁit]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[surrealist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist "Surrealist") artist known for his depictions of familiar objects in unfamiliar, unexpected contexts, which often provoked questions about the nature and boundaries of reality and representation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-1) His imagery has influenced [pop art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art"), [minimalist art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalist_art "Minimalist art"), and [conceptual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_art "Conceptual art").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Calvocoressi_1990,_p._26-2)
## Early life
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]
René Magritte was born in [Lessines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lessines "Lessines"), in the province of [Hainaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hainaut_\(province\) "Hainaut \(province\)") in Belgium, in 1898. He was the oldest son of Léopold Magritte, a tailor and textile merchant,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris216-3) and Régina (née Bertinchamps), who was a milliner before she got married. Little is known about Magritte's early life. He began lessons in drawing in 1910.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris216-3)
On 24 February 1912, his mother drowned herself in the [River Sambre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Sambre "River Sambre") at [Châtelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2telet,_Belgium "Châtelet, Belgium").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Abadie274-4) It was not her first suicide attempt. Her body was not discovered until 12 March, 16 days later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Abadie274-4) It was suggested that 13-year-old Magritte was present when her body was retrieved from the water, but later research discredited this story, which may have originated with the family nurse.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Cal9-5) Supposedly, when his mother was found, her dress was covering her face, an image that has been suggested as the source of several of Magritte's paintings in 1927–28 of people with cloth obscuring their faces, including _Les Amants_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-nga-6)
## Career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]
Magritte's earliest paintings, which date to about 1915, were [Impressionistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Cal9-5) In 1916–18, he studied at the [Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_Royale_des_Beaux-Arts "Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts")[Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Guggenheim-7) under [Constant Montald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_Montald "Constant Montald"), but found the instruction uninspiring.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Cal9-5) He also took classes at the Académie Royale from the painter and poster designer [Gisbert Combaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gisbert_Combaz "Gisbert Combaz").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-8) The paintings he produced between 1918 and 1924 were influenced by [Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism "Futurism") and the figurative [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism") of [Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Metzinger "Jean Metzinger").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Cal9-5)
From December 1920 to September 1921, Magritte served in the Belgian infantry in the [Flemish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") town of [Beverlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverlo "Beverlo") near [Leopoldsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldsburg "Leopoldsburg"). In 1922, he married Georgette Berger, whom he had met as a child in 1913.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris216-3) Also in 1922, the poet [Marcel Lecomte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Lecomte "Marcel Lecomte") showed Magritte a reproduction of [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico")'s _[The Song of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Love "The Song of Love")_ (painted in 1914). The work brought Magritte to tears; he described this as "one of the most moving moments of my life: my eyes _saw_ thought for the first time".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-9) The paintings of the Belgian symbolist painter [William Degouve de Nuncques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Degouve_de_Nuncques "William Degouve de Nuncques") have also been noted as an influence on Magritte, specifically _The Blind House_ (1892) and Magritte's variations or series on _The Empire of Lights_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Cassou_\(1984\)-10): 64–65 pp. 
In 1922–23, Magritte worked as a draughtsman in a wallpaper factory, and he was a poster and advertisement designer until 1926, when a contract with Galerie Le Centaure in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") made it possible for him to paint full-time. In 1926, Magritte produced his first surreal painting, _The Lost Jockey_ (_Le jockey perdu_).
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/54/The_Menaced_Assassin.jpg/250px-The_Menaced_Assassin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Menaced_Assassin.jpg)_[The Menaced Assassin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Menaced_Assassin "The Menaced Assassin")_ , 1927, [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/59/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_-_The_Lovers_%28Les_Amants%29_1928.jpg/250px-Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_-_The_Lovers_%28Les_Amants%29_1928.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_-_The_Lovers_\(Les_Amants\)_1928.jpg)_[The Lovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lovers_\(Magritte\) "The Lovers \(Magritte\)")_ , 1928, [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art")
In 1927 Magritte held his first solo exhibition, in Brussels.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Guggenheim-7) It had poor reviews;[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-11) depressed by the failure, he moved to Paris, where he became friends with [André Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Breton "André Breton") and became involved in the Surrealist group. An illusionistic, dream-like quality is characteristic of Magritte's version of Surrealism. He became a leading member of the movement and remained in Paris for three years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-rene-12) In 1929, he was put under contract at Goemans Gallery in Paris along with [Jean Arp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Arp "Jean Arp") and [Yves Tanguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Tanguy "Yves Tanguy").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-13)
On 15 December 1929, Magritte participated in the last publication, No. 12, of _[La Révolution surréaliste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_R%C3%A9volution_surr%C3%A9aliste "La Révolution surréaliste")_ , with his essay "Les mots et les images", where words play with images in sync with his work _[The Treachery of Images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Treachery_of_Images "The Treachery of Images")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-14)
Galerie Le Centaure closed at the end of 1929, ending Magritte's contract income. Having made little impact in Paris, Magritte returned to Brussels in 1930 and resumed working in advertising.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris217-15) He and his brother, Paul, formed an agency, which earned him a living wage. In 1932, Magritte joined the [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Belgium "Communist Party of Belgium"), which he periodically left and rejoined for several years.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris217-15) Between 1930 and 1932, Magritte had no exhibitions and sold no work.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Willsher-16) During this period, he was financially supported by a monthly stipend arranged by Belgian playwright Claude Spaak, the husband of [Suzanne Spaak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanne_Spaak "Suzanne Spaak"). In 1934, Suzanne Spaak's sister, Alice Lorge, purchased Magritte's _La Magie Noire_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Willsher-16) This was the first of a series of 11 paintings that depicted Magritte's wife, Georgette Berger, in a classical nude pose.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Willsher-16) Claude Spaak also commissioned portraits of his wife and children from Magritte.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Willsher-16)
In 1936, Magritte had his first solo exhibition in the United States, at the Julien Levy Gallery in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), followed by an exposition at the London Gallery in 1938.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-17)
Between 1934 and 1937, Magritte drew film posters under the pseudonym 'Emair' for the German sound film distributor [Tobis Klangfilm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobis-Klangfilm "Tobis-Klangfilm"). The Leuven City Archive preserves seven posters designed by Magritte.
During the early stages of his career, the British surrealist patron [Edward James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_James "Edward James") allowed Magritte to stay rent-free in his London home, where Magritte studied architecture and painted. James is depicted in two of Magritte's 1937 paintings, _Le Principe du Plaisir_ (_The Pleasure Principle_) and _La Reproduction Interdite_ , also known as _[Not to Be Reproduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_to_Be_Reproduced "Not to Be Reproduced")_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-18)
During the [German occupation of Belgium during World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_occupation_of_Belgium_during_World_War_II "German occupation of Belgium during World War II"), Magritte remained in Brussels, which led to a break with Breton. He briefly adopted a colorful, painterly style in 1943–44, an interlude known as his "[Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Auguste_Renoir "Pierre-Auguste Renoir") period", as a reaction to his feelings of alienation and abandonment living under German occupation.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-19)
In 1946, renouncing the violence and pessimism of his earlier work, he joined several other Belgian artists in signing the manifesto _Surrealism in Full Sunlight_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-20) During 1947–48, Magritte's "Vache period", he painted in a provocative and crude [Fauve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") style. During this time, he supported himself by producing fake Picassos, [Braques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Braque "Georges Braque"), and de Chiricos—a fraudulent repertoire he later expanded into the printing of forged banknotes during the lean postwar period. (Ironically, Belgium issued a 500-franc banknote celebrating Magritte on his centenary.) This venture was undertaken alongside his brother Paul and fellow Surrealist and "surrogate son" [Marcel Mariën](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Mari%C3%ABn "Marcel Mariën"), to whom had fallen the task of selling the forgeries.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-21) At the end of 1948, Magritte returned to the style and themes of his pre-war surrealistic art.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-22)
In France, Magritte's work has been showcased in a number of retrospective exhibitions, including at the [Centre Georges Pompidou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_Georges_Pompidou "Centre Georges Pompidou") in 2016 and 2017. In the U.S., his work has been displayed in three retrospective exhibitions: at the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in 1965, the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in 1992, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art again in 2013. The 2018 exhibition, "The Fifth Season" at the [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art"), focused on the work of his later years.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-23)
Politically, Magritte stood to the left, and retained close ties to the Communist Party, even in the postwar years. But he was critical of the functionalist cultural policy of the Communist left, saying, "Class consciousness is as necessary as bread; but that does not mean that workers must be condemned to bread and water and that wanting chicken and champagne would be harmful. [...] For the Communist painter, the justification of artistic activity is to create pictures that can represent mental luxury." While remaining committed to the political left, he thus advocated a certain autonomy of art.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-25) Magritte was an agnostic in religious belief.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-26)
Popular interest in Magritte's work rose considerably in the 1960s, and his imagery has influenced [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art"), [minimalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalist_art "Minimalist art"), and [conceptual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_art "Conceptual art").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Calvocoressi_1990,_p._26-2) In 2005, he was ranked ninth in the [Walloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Community_of_Belgium "French Community of Belgium") popular vote on _[Les plus grands Belges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_plus_grands_Belges "Les plus grands Belges")_ ("The greatest Belgians");[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-27) in the [Flemish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") version, _[De Grootste Belg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Grootste_Belg "De Grootste Belg")_ , he was 18th.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-28)
## Personal life
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]
In June 1922, Magritte married Georgette Berger, the daughter of a butcher in Charleroi. They had first met when she was 13 and he was 15; they met again in Brussels in 1920[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-mattesonbiog-29) and Georgette, who had also studied art, became Magritte's model, muse, and wife.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-30)
In 1936, Magritte's marriage became troubled when he met a young performance artist, [Sheila Legge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheila_Legge "Sheila Legge"), and began an affair with her. Magritte arranged for his friend Paul Colinet to entertain and distract Georgette, but this led to an affair between Georgette and Colinet. Magritte and his wife did not reconcile until 1940.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-31)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]
Magritte died of [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") on 15 August 1967, aged 68, and was interred in [Schaerbeek Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaerbeek_Cemetery "Schaerbeek Cemetery"), [Evere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evere "Evere"), Brussels.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-32)
## Philosophical and artistic gestures
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Philosophical and artistic gestures")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b6/The_Empire_of_Light_MOMA.jpg/330px-The_Empire_of_Light_MOMA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Empire_of_Light_MOMA.jpg)_[The Empire of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empire_of_Light "The Empire of Light")_ , c. 1950–1954, [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art")
> It is a union that suggests the essential mystery of the world. Art for me is not an end in itself, but a means of evoking that mystery.
— René Magritte on putting seemingly unrelated objects together in juxtaposition[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-33)
Magritte's work frequently displays a collection of ordinary objects in an unusual context, giving new meanings to familiar things. The use of objects as other than what they seem typifies his work.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-34) For example, _[The Treachery of Images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Treachery_of_Images "The Treachery of Images")_ (_La trahison des images_) shows a [pipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoking_pipe_\(tobacco\) "Smoking pipe \(tobacco\)") that looks as though it is a model for a tobacco store advertisement. Magritte painted below the pipe "_Ceci n'est pas une pipe_ " ("This is not a pipe"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-35) which seems a contradiction but is actually true: the painting is not a pipe, it is an _image_ of a pipe. It does not "satisfy emotionally"; asked about this image, Magritte said that of course it was not a pipe—just try to fill it with tobacco.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-36)

Magritte's work has been described by [Suzi Gablik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzi_Gablik "Suzi Gablik") as "a systematic attempt to disrupt any dogmatic view of the physical world".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-37) Therefore, when Magritte painted rocks—which are commonly understood to be heavy, inanimate objects—he often painted them floating cloud-like in the sky, or painted scenes of people and their environment turned to stone.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-38)
Among Magritte's works are a number of surrealist versions of other famous paintings, such as _Perspective I_ and _Perspective II_ , which are copies of [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Louis_David "Jacques-Louis David")'s _[Portrait of Madame Récamier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Madame_R%C3%A9camier "Portrait of Madame Récamier")_[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-NGCPerspectiveIAndMadameRecamier-39) and [Manet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manet "Manet")'s _[The Balcony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Balcony_\(Manet\) "The Balcony \(Manet\)")_ ,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-MSKGentPerspectiveIIAndBalcony-40) respectively, with the human subjects replaced by coffins.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-41) Elsewhere, Magritte challenges the difficulty of artwork to convey meaning with a recurring motif of an easel, as in his _The Human Condition_ series (1933, 1935) or _The Promenades of Euclid_ (1955), wherein the spires of a castle are "painted" upon the ordinary streets the canvas overlooks. In a letter to Breton, he wrote of _The Human Condition_ that it was irrelevant if the scene behind the easel differed from what was depicted upon it, "but the main thing was to eliminate the difference between a view seen from outside and from inside a room".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-42) The windows in some of these pictures are framed with heavy drapes, suggesting a theatrical motif.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-43)
Magritte's style of surrealism is more representational than the ["automatic"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist_automatism "Surrealist automatism") style of artists such as [Joan Miró](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Mir%C3%B3 "Joan Miró"). His use of ordinary objects in unfamiliar spaces is joined to his desire to create poetic imagery. He called painting "the art of putting colors side by side in such a way that their real aspect is effaced, so that familiar objects—the sky, people, trees, mountains, furniture, the stars, solid structures, graffiti—become united in a single poetically disciplined image. The poetry of this image dispenses with any symbolic significance, old or new."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-44)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Magritte_treachery.jpg/250px-Magritte_treachery.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magritte_treachery.jpg)_[The Treachery of Images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Treachery_of_Images "The Treachery of Images") (This Is Not A Pipe/Ceci n'est pas une pipe)_, 1929, by René Magritte
Magritte described his paintings as "visible images which conceal nothing; they evoke mystery and, indeed, when one sees one of my pictures, one asks oneself this simple question, 'What does that mean?'. It does not mean anything, because mystery means nothing either, it is unknowable."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-45)
Magritte's constant play with reality and illusion has been attributed to the early death of his mother. Psychoanalysts who have examined bereaved children have hypothesized that Magritte's back-and-forth play with reality and illusion reflects his "constant shifting back and forth from what he wishes—'mother is alive'—to what he knows—'mother is dead'".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-46)
In 2019 Patricia Allmer demonstrated the influence of fairground attractions on Magritte's art, from carousels and circuses to panoramas and stage magic.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-47)
## Artists influenced by Magritte
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Artists influenced by Magritte")]
Contemporary artists have been greatly influenced by Magritte's examination of the fickleness of images. Artists influenced by Magritte include [John Baldessari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Baldessari "John Baldessari"), [Ed Ruscha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Ruscha "Ed Ruscha"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), [Jasper Johns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasper_Johns "Jasper Johns"), [Jan Verdoodt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Verdoodt "Jan Verdoodt"), [Martin Kippenberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kippenberger "Martin Kippenberger"), [Duane Michals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Michals "Duane Michals"), [Storm Thorgerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Thorgerson "Storm Thorgerson"), and [Luis Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Rey_\(artist\) "Luis Rey \(artist\)"). Some of their works integrate direct references and others offer contemporary viewpoints on his abstract fixations.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-48)
Magritte's use of simple graphic and everyday imagery has been compared to that of [pop artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art"). His influence in the development of pop art has been widely recognized,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris202-49) although Magritte himself discounted the connection. He considered the pop artists' representation of "the world as it is" as "their error", and contrasted their attention to the transitory with his concern for "the feeling for the real, insofar as it is permanent."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Meuris202-49) The 2006–07 [LACMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LACMA "LACMA") exhibition "Magritte and Contemporary Art: The Treachery of Images" examined the relationship between Magritte and contemporary art.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-50)

## Magritte Museum and other collections
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_Magritte&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Magritte Museum and other collections")]
Main article: [Magritte Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magritte_Museum "Magritte Museum")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Liebenau_-_Die_Beschaffenheit_des_Menschen_%28Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_1933%29.jpg/250px-Liebenau_-_Die_Beschaffenheit_des_Menschen_%28Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_1933%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Liebenau_-_Die_Beschaffenheit_des_Menschen_\(Ren%C3%A9_Magritte_1933\).jpg)The copy of Magritte's _[The Human Condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Human_Condition_\(Magritte\) "The Human Condition \(Magritte\)")_ , on the facade of the New Middle School in Liebenau, Freistadt district
The Magritte Museum opened to the public on 30 May 2009 in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-62) Housed in the five-level neo-classical Hotel Altenloh, on the Place Royale, it displays some 200 original Magritte paintings, drawings, and sculptures,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-63) including _The Return_ , _Scheherazade_ and _[The Empire of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empire_of_Light "The Empire of Light")_.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-64) This multidisciplinary permanent installation is the biggest Magritte archive anywhere and most of the work is directly from the collection of the artist's widow, [Georgette Magritte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgette_Berger "Georgette Berger"), and from [Irene Hamoir Scutenaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ir%C3%A8ne_Hamoir "Irène Hamoir"), his primary collector.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Oisteanu-65) Additionally, the museum includes Magritte's experiments with photography from 1920 on and the short Surrealist films he made from 1956 on.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-Oisteanu-65)
Another museum is at 135 Rue Esseghem in Brussels, Magritte's former home, where he lived with his wife from 1930 to 1954. _Olympia_ (1948), a nude portrait of Magritte's wife reportedly worth about US$1.1 million, was stolen from this museum on the morning of 24 September 2009 by two armed men.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-68) It was returned to the museum in January 2012 in exchange for a 50,000-Euro payment from the museum's insurer. The thieves reportedly agreed to the deal because they could not sell the painting on the [black market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_market "Black market") due to its fame.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-69)
The [Menil Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menil_Collection "Menil Collection") in Houston, Texas, holds one of the most significant collections of dada and surrealist work in the United States, including dozens of oil paintings, gouaches, drawings, and bronzes by Magritte. [John de Menil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Menil "John de Menil") and [Dominique de Menil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_de_Menil "Dominique de Menil") initiated and funded the [catalogue raisonné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalogue_raisonn%C3%A9 "Catalogue raisonné") of Magritte's oeuvre, published between 1992 and 1997 in five volumes, with an addendum in 2012. Major oil paintings in the Menil Collection include _[The Meaning of Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Meaning_of_Night_\(painting\) "The Meaning of Night \(painting\)")_ (1927), _The Eternally Obvious_ (1930), _The Rape_ (1934), _[The Listening Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Listening_Room "The Listening Room")_ (1952), and _[Golconda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golconda_\(Magritte\) "Golconda \(Magritte\)")_ (1953). They are typically exhibited a few at a time on a rotating basis with other surrealist works in the collection.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte#cite_note-70)
